analysis.one_liner: Taxes coal $10 a ton to fund community protection along coal rail routes and require covered coal cars.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a $10 per ton tax on coal extracted in the United States and put the money into a new Coal Mitigation Trust Fund [S2][S3]. States that ship at least 2.5 million tons of coal by rail a year could draw on the fund to deal with the noise, vibration, traffic, pollution, and emergencies that come with coal trains, and to help coal workers retrain [S2][S3]. It would also require the Transportation Department to write rules so coal rail cars are covered or otherwise treated so coal dust does not escape in transit [S2][S3]. A separate provision lengthens the tax depreciation period for coal export port property to 50 years, which reduces the tax benefit investors get from building those ports [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: People living along rail corridors in states that move at least 2.5 million tons of coal a year by rail, who bear the noise, dust, and traffic of coal trains, would get money for mitigation. Coal workers facing job loss would get adjustment assistance [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Coal Mitigation Trust Fund funded by a $10 per ton excise tax on coal extraction, available to states to mitigate noise, vibration, traffic delays, pollution, and other public health threats from coal transport by rail [S2][S3].
Makes trust fund money available for worker adjustment assistance for people affected by changes in the coal industry [S2][S3].
Directs the Secretary of Transportation to require all coal rail cars to be covered or use alternative technology so coal dust does not escape during transport [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mining companies would pay the $10 per ton tax, a cost they would pass through in the price of coal, ultimately reaching electricity customers and industrial users. Investors in coal export port infrastructure would get slower tax write-offs under the 50-year depreciation period [S3].

drawbacks.text: The $10 per ton tax applies to all coal extracted in the United States, not only coal that is transported through affected communities, so much of the cost would fall on electricity and steel customers nationwide rather than only where the burden is [S3].
The tax would raise the price of coal as an input, which flows through to household energy bills and energy-intensive manufacturing, an honest supporter would have to acknowledge this cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, localized burden—coal dust, noise, and traffic on rail-adjacent communities—and funds it with a tax on the product causing it, plus dust controls that address the problem at the source. The main design weakness is that the tax hits all coal, spreading part of the cost to energy consumers everywhere rather than only in the communities that bear the transport burden.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 2012 and referred to the Ways and Means and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Jim McDermott on July 25, 2012, with four Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the day it was introduced [S5].
Two subcommittees of the Transportation Committee received referrals on July 26, 2012, but no markup, hearing vote, or floor action ever followed [S5].
No further action appears in the record through the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mining companies kept $10 per ton they would have owed under the tax, coal exporters kept the faster depreciation treatment, and the communities along coal rail routes got no mitigation funding or dust controls. The committees that held the bill also avoided setting any precedent for taxing coal extraction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal producers, exporters, and rail shippers

for.name: Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its $10 per ton coal extraction tax, trust fund, and coal car dust rules.

for.name: Barbara Lee, Mike Honda, Charles Rangel, and Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original sponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral; no markup or vote appears in the record.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of secondary referral (rail and port provisions)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two subcommittees and never acted on it; no markup or vote appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, but all five sponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled committees it was referred to never scheduled any action on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: A $10 per ton excise tax on extraction would come directly out of the industry's margin on roughly a billion tons of annual U.S. production, passed partly to energy consumers. The industry's cost is the fund that pays for the communities its transport burdens.

industries.industry: Coal export ports and terminal investors
industries.note: The bill lengthens the depreciation recovery period for coal port property to 50 years, slowing the tax write-offs investors can take on export terminals. This removes a tax advantage for expanding coal exports.

Covered-car rules would impose equipment costs on railroads hauling coal, and the 50-year recovery period would also slow write-offs on railroad grading. Mitigation funds would flow to states rather than to the railroads themselves.
